para-006: When clients report being routed to the wrong server address, check for a stale DNS resolver cache returning outdated records before investigating network or routing config. Flushing the resolver cache or lowering TTLs resolves it.
para-014: Constant socket opening and closing pointed to connection churn caused by misconfigured keepalive settings. The fix was tuning TCP/application keepalive timeouts so connections persist instead of being torn down repeatedly.
para-025: Parallel requests queueing while CPU sits idle indicates thread pool starvation under fan-out: blocking calls exhaust the worker pool and requests wait despite idle CPU. Diagnose by comparing CPU utilization with request queue depth and fix by increasing/segmenting the thread pool or removing blocking calls.
para-032: Urgent tasks waiting behind batch work was scheduler priority inversion. Keep standard priority-inversion mitigations in mind: priority inheritance, isolating batch jobs from the interactive path, and never holding a resource a high-priority task needs.
para-038: Duplicate identifiers appearing in traces were caused by a request ID counter overflowing and wrapping back to previously issued IDs. Use sufficiently wide ID spaces or reset counters only when the namespace is exhausted-safe.
para-039: A CSV download showing broken characters is a charset mismatch garbling the export file. Ensure the export byte encoding and the response Content-Type charset header agree (e.g., UTF-8 everywhere, with a BOM if Excel requires it).
para-049: Brief drops in inter-system calls were caused by the service mesh sidecar restarting under memory pressure. Treat sidecar OOMs as a cause of intermittent RPC failures; raise the sidecar memory limit and investigate pressure sources.
para-054: A process unable to open new sockets can be a full file descriptor table during a connection storm. Check open FD counts (often thousands of unclosed sockets) with lsof/ulimit first; raise the limit and fix connection leaks.
para-057: Read latency degrading over time can be compaction backlog accumulating on the storage engine, with reads paying growing write-amplification costs. Monitor compaction progress vs. write rate and throttle or add capacity when backlog grows.
para-059: A cache miss storm overloaded the origin because request coalescing failed under a thundering herd: concurrent misses for the same key all fetched independently. Defend with lock-based single-flight dedup, jittered TTLs, and early background refresh of hot keys.
para-060: A cluster shrinking for no reason was caused by the heartbeat timeout evicting healthy members that were slow or briefly unresponsive rather than dead. Lengthen or adapt the heartbeat timeout and require confirmation before eviction to avoid false removals.
para-061: Vanished bandwidth savings traced to the payload compression ratio collapsing on binary blobs, which are already dense and barely compress. Detect incompressible payloads and skip or switch compression for them instead of compressing everything uniformly.
para-072: Events arriving out of order after a partition rebalance indicate per-partition ordering guarantees broke when keys were reassigned. Keep ordering-sensitive messages keyed to the same partition across rebalances or add sequence numbers for consumer-side reordering.
para-073: Returning visitors performing a full TLS handshake means session resumption failed across server restarts, since session tickets/cache state was lost. Persist or share session ticket keys (and, where used, session cache) across instances so resumption survives restarts.
para-075: Capacity flapping up and down is classic autoscaler oscillation: nodes added, load dropped, nodes removed repeatedly. Use hysteresis, longer stabilization windows, and scale-up/down asymmetry to damp the feedback loop.
para-076: A single page load firing hundreds of database queries is the GraphQL resolver N+1 problem: each field resolver issues its own query. Batch/deduplicate at the data layer (e.g., DataLoader) by grouping per-field batched lookups per request.
para-077: The origin absorbing full traffic after a deploy means cache-stampede protection misfired — the new deployment invalidated or broke the coalescing/lock layer, letting a thundering herd of misses through. Verify stampede guards still function after deploys and warm the cache before switching traffic.
para-080: When everything feels slow but nothing is outright broken, check latency trends rather than point-in-time health: p99 had crept upward all week. Track p95/p99 trendlines against a baseline to catch gradual regressions instead of waiting for hard failures.
para-081: Considering freezing releases means the error budget is burning faster than planned. Respond by throttling change velocity, prioritizing reliability fixes over features, and reviewing what is consuming the budget before it drains.
para-082: Disagreeing report numbers can come from the overnight batch finishing at different times or partially, so reports read inconsistent snapshot states. Make consumers aware of batch completion state and read from a consistent, post-batch snapshot before trusting or comparing numbers.
para-083: When nothing reproduces but users report intermittent complaints since Tuesday, correlate symptom onset with a specific point-in-time change (deploy, config, DNS, isopdate) around that date instead of re-running repro attempts. Time-anchored diffing of changes is the investigation path.
para-084: A dashboard flapping red-then-green with no deploy points to infrastructure/trend noise rather than a deployment cause. Check external factors (dependency flakiness, load, alarms at thresholds) and suppress or damp alerts that self-recover.
para-085: A quiet breakage that only surfaced as a support-ticket spike after a holiday shows failure detection lagging users. Set up internal failure monitors so regressions are caught by signals, not by customer complaints.
para-086: 'Works on staging, fails in production' means config/parity drift between environments, not the code. Diff production vs staging configuration, data, scale and network topology to find theenvironment-specific factor.
para-087: The same alert firing three nights running caused paging fatigue; treat repeated identical pages as needing a root-cause fix, not repeated acknowledgment. Deduplicate/narrow the alert and add auto-resolution so honest signals survive
para-088: Flat graphs after a successful deploy raise the question of whether traffic actually flowed; verify ingress counters and real user traffic before assuming the deploy is broken. Pipeline-stage instrumentation (deploy -> traffic -> metric propagation delay) helps distinguish deploy failure from dashboardsupdate lag.
para-089: A vague escalated complaint from customer success on a big account needs a structured intake: request concrete impacts (timestamps, IDs, error messages) before engineering investigates; triage by account importance but not by asserted severity.
para-090: Getting paged twice after midnight shows noisy overnight alerts eroding sleep and trust; batch or defer non-urgent alerts and reserve overnight pages for actionable ones. Review alert thresholds to ensurethe page justifies waking someone.
para-098: Holiday traffic dwarfing load-test numbers means production traffic forecasts let people down; ground capacity planning on historical holiday peaks rather than baseline load tests, and add margin over the largest observed spike before the next surge.
para-099: Postmortem action items rot when assigned to 'nobody in particular.' Assign each item a named owner with a deadline and track it in the normal work backlog so follow-through is visible.
